title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Unit 101
description: Bureaucratic register and red tape: formal administrative wording, official correspondence, accessible plain-English equivalents, and relevant word families.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using a user-supplied textbook as the vocabulary reference. Vocabulary items were checked against the teaching pages, exercises and answer key. All example sentences, notes and translations are newly written; textbook passages and exercise texts are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 101, printed pages 208–209 (PDF pages 210–211), covering sections A–B, exercises 101.1–101.5 and the answer key on PDF pages 276–277.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA provided only for short targets where reasonably reliable; longer expressions have blank IPA rather than invented connected-speech transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing text is in English, except Brazilian Portuguese translations stored in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared printed and PDF pages, read both teaching and exercise pages, consulted Unit 101 answers and word-family table, checked nuanced meanings/register/prepositions and wrote original examples. Static JSON/schema, IDs and audio-target checks were performed; browser integration testing was not performed.
audit.limitations: The package contains no recorded MP3s. Browser import, pronunciation scoring and live Word/Sentence TTS were not tested. Highly formal expressions and legal terminology can vary between jurisdictions; clarifiable is rare despite appearing in the word-formation key.

units.title: Unit 101 — Red tape
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 208–209 (PDF pages 210–211).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Language variation · bureaucratic register, correspondence and plain English
learningObjectives: Recognise inflated, impersonal and passive constructions characteristic of bureaucratic English.
Translate formal administrative verbs and expressions into natural everyday alternatives without losing precision.
Use conventional forms for correspondence, requests, notices and appeals with appropriate preposition patterns.
Recognise key word families such as clarify/clarification and rectify/rectification, including uncommon derived adjectives.

sectionsChecked: A · Characteristics of bureaucratic language (sample notices, explanations and vocabulary)
Answer key for Unit 101, including alternative plain-English answers

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Small businesses complain that red tape delays the approval of new licences.
items.note: An informal, usually disapproving expression for excessive administrative rules or procedures; not literally a kind of tape.

items.pt: linguagem burocrática; linguagem administrativa excessivamente formal
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The council rewrote the notice to remove unnecessary bureaucratic language.
items.note: Refers to the formal, often indirect and impersonal register of administration.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Under the agreement, each party shall maintain accurate records.
items.note: A traditional legal and contractual modal; often expresses obligation, not ordinary prediction. Modern plain-language drafting often prefers must or will depending on meaning.

items.pt: ter direito a; ser elegível para
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Applicants may be eligible for financial assistance if they meet the criteria.
items.note: Formal expression for meeting the requirements for a benefit or opportunity; eligible is followed by for.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The agency requested further information in relation to the application.
items.note: Formal link meaning concerning; can often be replaced by about, depending on context.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The applicant must have attained the required age by the closing date.
items.note: Formal verb, particularly for ages, standards and qualifications; often replaces reach.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The foundation bestowed an award on the researcher for her discoveries.
items.note: Typically used of honours, prizes or privileges formally given to a person; also bestow something upon someone.
items.speechText: bestow an award on a scientist

items.pt: ser concedido a; ser outorgado a
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The distinction was bestowed on a scientist whose work changed the field.
items.note: Passive form particularly frequent in formal descriptions of awards and honours.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The owners applied for permission to demolish the old warehouse.
items.note: Formal or technical verb for knocking down a building; also used figuratively of arguments.

items.pt: contíguo; vizinho; que fica ao lado
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The company bought an adjoining plot to expand its facilities.
items.note: Formal adjective referring to property or land immediately next to something.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The owner was required to give access to the property for an inspection.
items.note: In official correspondence, property may refer to a house, land or other real estate, rather than simply home.

items.pt: por meio deste documento; pelo presente
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: I hereby confirm that the information supplied is accurate.
items.note: Very formal adverb used to state that a document or utterance performs an official action.

items.pt: ser indeferido por meio deste comunicado
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The application is hereby rejected because the supporting documents are incomplete.
items.note: Passive legal-administrative formula; plain English often uses we have rejected your application.

items.pt: o signatário; a pessoa que assina o documento
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The undersigned confirms receipt of the original contract.
items.note: Formal noun phrase referring to whoever signs a letter or document.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The aforementioned documents must be provided before the hearing.
items.note: Highly formal adjective meaning already mentioned; often replaceable by these or the documents mentioned above.

items.pt: todo e qualquer; todos, sem exceção
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The policy requires disclosure of any and all relevant conflicts of interest.
items.note: Legalistic intensifying phrase; the shorter all often conveys the same meaning.

items.pt: apresentar um recurso; protocolar uma contestação
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Residents may submit an appeal within thirty days of the decision.
items.note: Formal administrative collocation; the appeal challenges a decision.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The tribunal issued guidance in respect of the new regulations.
items.note: Formal British-style wording meaning concerning; meaning can vary in legal contexts.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Construction is expected to commence early next spring.
items.note: Formal alternative to begin or start, frequent in notices and regulations.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Payment is due before the commencement of the course.
items.note: Noun form of commence, especially in official documents.

items.pt: encerrar as atividades; interromper as operações
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The subsidiary ceased operations after the merger.
items.note: Formal phrase indicating that an organisation has stopped functioning; the context determines whether the closure is permanent.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The supplier was ordered to cease production until the safety issue was resolved.
items.note: Formal alternative to stop; can be transitive or intransitive.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The agreement provides for the cessation of deliveries during an emergency.
items.note: Formal noun describing the end or stopping of an activity or process.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The deceased had left clear instructions in the will.
items.note: Formal, especially legal or administrative expression referring to a person who has died.

items.pt: parente mais próximo; familiar de referência
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The hospital asked the patient to provide contact details for their next of kin.
items.note: A contact or relative identified as close to someone; legal rights associated with next of kin depend on jurisdiction.

items.pt: em caso de; na eventualidade de
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: In the event of a power failure, the backup system will start automatically.
items.note: Formal conditional phrase; if there is often sounds more natural in everyday instructions.
items.speechText: in the event of a fire

items.pt: evacuar; retirar pessoas de um local
items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Staff evacuated the building after the fire alarm sounded.
items.note: In active form, people evacuate a building; in passive form, a building can be evacuated.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The contractor will endeavour to resolve the issue within five working days.
items.note: Formal British spelling of endeavor; endeavour to do something is less direct than promise to do it.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The new process should facilitate access to public services.
items.note: Formal transitive verb, often followed by a noun or -ing form; not usually followed directly by an infinitive.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The department instructed contractors to suspend work immediately.
items.note: Often means to give official directions; instruct someone to do something.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Once the documents have been checked, we can proceed to the next stage.
items.note: Formal way of indicating progress to a subsequent stage or action; proceed to do something is also possible.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: The supplier must rectify the error before the invoice is approved.
items.note: Formal alternative to correct or put right, common for errors and administrative problems.

items.section: A · Formal wording in official texts
items.example: Normal service will resume once the repairs have been completed.
items.note: Formal verb meaning begin again after a pause; not the noun résumé meaning a CV.

items.pt: confirmar o recebimento de; acusar recebimento de
items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: Please acknowledge receipt of the attached documents by Friday.
items.note: Formal correspondence formula confirming that something arrived; receipt here is a noun.

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: The office acknowledged the complaint but did not respond to its substance.
items.note: In formal correspondence, acknowledge can mean confirm receipt; in other contexts it can mean admit or recognise.

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: The sample was sent with the compliments of the manufacturer.
items.note: Conventional formula on a card or slip sent with a complimentary item; not necessarily an intimate personal greeting.
items.speechText: with the compliments of the publisher

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: You must notify the authority of any change in your circumstances.
items.note: Formal synonym of inform; common patterns are notify someone of something and notify someone that ... .

items.pt: assim que possível; quando lhe for conveniente
items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: Please return the signed form at your earliest convenience.
items.note: Polite but formal request for a prompt response; not specifically early in the morning.

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: We requested clarification of the eligibility criteria.
items.note: Formal noun for making something clearer; further clarification is a common administrative collocation.

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: Please contact the office if further clarification is required.
items.note: A conventional formal phrase; you need more information often sounds more natural in everyday language.

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: I enclose a copy of the signed agreement for your records.
items.note: Traditional letter-writing verb for including a document, usually physically; attach is more usual for email attachments.

items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: The finance team requested payment in respect of an outstanding invoice.
items.note: Illustrates the correspondence use of in respect of meaning relating to; invoice is a formal bill requesting payment.

items.pt: com relação a; a respeito de
items.section: B · Bureaucratic correspondence
items.example: I am writing with regard to the decision communicated last week.
items.note: Formal linking phrase meaning about or concerning; avoid using regarding to.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: Passengers were asked to await instructions before disembarking.
items.note: Formal alternative to wait for instructions; await is transitive and does not take for.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: All suppliers must comply with the safety regulations.
items.note: Formal phrase used for obeying rules, regulations or laws; comply is followed by with.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: The new regulations require operators to keep maintenance records.
items.note: Official rules that govern an activity; obey the rules is the plain-English equivalent of comply with regulations.

items.pt: inserir moedas; colocar moedas na abertura indicada
items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: Insert coins into the machine before selecting a ticket.
items.note: Formal instruction; in everyday instructions put coins in may sound simpler.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: The investigator concluded that the allegation was without foundation.
items.note: Formal phrase meaning unsupported by evidence; close to unfounded or unjustified depending on context.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: Visitors are requested to refrain from taking photographs.
items.note: Formal polite prohibition; followed by a noun or -ing form, never a bare infinitive.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: Please state your country of residence on the application form.
items.note: Administrative term for the country where you live, not necessarily your nationality or citizenship.

items.section: Exercises 101.2–101.5 · Formal-to-plain English
items.example: The panel found the complaint unjustified after reviewing the evidence.
items.note: Can describe something lacking sufficient reason; overlaps with unfounded but is not identical in every context.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The official clarified the deadline after receiving several questions.
items.note: Verb related to clarification and the uncommon adjective clarifiable.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The wording is clarifiable, although a complete rewrite would be better.
items.note: Listed in the book’s word-family exercise; grammatically possible but uncommon in natural English. It can be clarified is usually more idiomatic.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: A neutral mediator provided facilitation during the negotiations.
items.note: Noun for the process of making something easier or helping a group proceed.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The report identified several facilitating factors in the approval process.
items.note: Present participle of facilitate; may function as a modifier before a noun.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The officer issued an instruction to suspend operations.
items.note: Noun from instruct; can be countable for a particular direction or uncountable for teaching.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The comparison was particularly instructive for new staff.
items.note: Adjective meaning helpful in teaching or explaining; it is not simply the same as instructed.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The applicant received notification of the outcome by email.
items.note: Noun from notify; describes an official message or the act of notifying.

items.pt: de notificação obrigatória; que deve ser comunicado
items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: Certain diseases are classified as notifiable by public-health authorities.
items.note: Means subject to a legal or official notification requirement; the precise requirement depends on context.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The authority requested rectification of the errors in the application.
items.note: Formal noun from rectify, particularly common in technical, legal and administrative settings.

items.section: Exercise 101.4 · Word formation
items.example: The engineer confirmed that the defect was rectifiable without replacing the equipment.
items.note: Adjective meaning capable of being corrected or put right.
